1. I will exploit the 1990 federal random draw: run a city-level IV of post-draw (2000 and 2010) direct general expenditure per resident on the entropy segregation index, instrumented by `audit_grant`, with state-by-year fixed effects. The sample is the 40 eligible cities over 100,000 residents in the two participating states.
2. The draw is randomized, and the grant paid a nonprofit rather than the city and "changed nothing else." That makes independence and exclusion credible, so I will lead with the reduced-form effect of the draw on spending.
3. I rejected `waterways` despite its strong first stage of 1.5 points per waterway. Streams set school-district and municipal boundaries, so more waterways mean more fragmented local government, which affects city spending directly and violates exclusion.
4. The main threat is a very weak instrument: the first-stage F is about 2, there are only 40 cities, and the shift is just 0.3 index points. Conventional 2SLS would be biased toward OLS with misleading standard errors, so I will report only Anderson-Rubin (weak-IV-robust) confidence sets and randomization-inference p-values.
5. I expect the confidence set to be wide and possibly unbounded. The estimate is also a local effect for large cities in two states, so I will report it as a credible but probably uninformative bound rather than a precise national effect.
6. Other key variables are `log_pop`, `pct_black`, `pct_hisp`, `med_income`, `own_rate` and `region`, entered only as pre-1990 baseline covariates for precision, plus spending deflated to real dollars.

CANDIDATES:
waterways | violated
audit_grant | plausible
INSTRUMENT: audit_grant

**Plan**

1. Neither candidate instrument supports credible IV estimation, so I will not use one. `waterways` moves segregation (about 1.5 points per stream), but every counted stream became a 1920 jurisdiction line. Cities with more streams therefore sit in more fragmented systems of school districts and municipalities, and that fragmentation can change city spending directly, which violates the exclusion restriction. `audit_grant` was randomly assigned and paid a nonprofit rather than the city, so exclusion is plausible. But it covers only 40 large cities in two states and has a first-stage F of about 2, so 2SLS would be badly biased and its inference unreliable.
2. My main design is therefore a city panel for 1980–2010. I will regress real direct general expenditure per resident (CPI-deflated) on the entropy segregation index. The model includes city fixed effects and state-by-year fixed effects, controls for log_pop, pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income and own_rate, and clusters standard errors by city. Identification then comes from within-city changes in segregation relative to other cities in the same state and year.
3. As a supplement, I will report the `audit_grant` reduced form and an Anderson–Rubin confidence interval, which stays valid under a weak instrument. I expect this interval to be wide, so I treat it as a check rather than the headline estimate.
4. The main threat is time-varying confounding that the fixed effects do not absorb. Examples are white flight driven by local economic decline, or spending changes that themselves move residents and alter segregation (reverse causality). I will probe this with lead tests (future segregation should not predict current spending) and coefficient-stability sensitivity bounds in the style of Oster.

CANDIDATES:
waterways | violated
audit_grant | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: NONE

**Plan.** I will estimate the effect by two-stage least squares, using the number of waterways crossing each city as the instrument for its multigroup entropy segregation index. Following the stated first stage, both stages include state-by-year fixed effects and log_pop, which yields about 1.5 index points per waterway. I will add pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income, own_rate and land area as controls, deflate the outcome to real per-resident direct general expenditure, and cluster standard errors by city. The main threat is the exclusion restriction: rivers may raise or lower spending directly through bridges, roads, flood control, sewerage and their historical role in industrial and population growth, not only through segregation. To probe this, I will re-estimate using spending categories rivers should not affect (e.g., police, parks, administration), check whether waterways predict pre-1980 spending, and test sensitivity to controlling for water area and historical city size. I rejected audit_grant even though it was randomized: it covers only 40 large cities in two states and has a first-stage F of about 2, so it is too weak for useful inference. The codebook's other fields are unlabeled administrative items with no stated link to segregation, so I did not treat any of them as instruments.

CANDIDATES:
waterways | plausible
audit_grant | violated
INSTRUMENT: waterways

I would not use an instrumental-variables design here, because neither candidate instrument is usable. `waterways` strongly predicts segregation (about 1.5 points per stream). However, streams also set the boundaries of school districts and municipalities, so more waterways means more separately governed jurisdictions. That fragmentation plausibly affects per-resident spending directly, which violates exclusion. `audit_grant` was randomly assigned and changed nothing else, so exclusion is believable, but it covers only 40 cities and has a first-stage F of about 2. With so little strength, 2SLS would be biased toward OLS and give uninformative intervals, so at most I would report its reduced form and an Anderson–Rubin confidence set as a side check. The main design is therefore a city-level panel for 1980–2010 of real direct general expenditure per resident (CPI-deflated) on the entropy index, with city fixed effects, state-by-year fixed effects, and time-varying controls (`log_pop`, `pct_black`, `pct_hisp`, `med_income`, `own_rate`), with standard errors clustered by city. The main threat is time-varying confounding, such as economic decline that raises segregation and cuts budgets together, which I will probe with pre-trend checks and sensitivity bounds; results should be read as conditional associations, not clean causal effects.

CANDIDATES:
waterways | violated
audit_grant | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: NONE

**Plan.** I will not use `waterways` as the instrument. The program documentation says every 1920 boundary stream became a jurisdiction line, so more streams mean more separately governed municipalities and school districts. Fragmentation can change city spending directly, through fiscal competition, scale and service assignment, so the exclusion restriction fails even with state-by-year fixed effects and log population.

Instead, I will instrument segregation with `audit_grant`. It was a federal random draw among the 40 cities over 100,000 residents in the two participating states, the grant went to a nonprofit rather than the city government, and it reportedly changed nothing else, so independence and exclusion are plausible. The design is 2SLS on the 2000 and 2010 city-years for those 40 cities:
- **Outcome:** CPI-deflated direct general expenditure per resident.
- **Endogenous variable:** the entropy segregation index.
- **Controls:** state-by-year fixed effects, plus pre-draw 1980/1990 values of `log_pop`, `pct_black`, `pct_hisp`, `med_income` and `own_rate` for precision only.
- **Inference:** standard errors clustered by city.

The main threat is a weak instrument. The first stage is only about −0.3 index points with F ≈ 2 on 40 clusters. I will therefore report Anderson-Rubin confidence sets and the reduced-form effect of the draw on spending, rather than conventional 2SLS t-tests, and I expect those intervals to be wide and possibly unbounded. Any estimate is also a local effect for large cities in two states.

audit_grant | plausible
INSTRUMENT: audit_grant

**Plan**

1. I will use the 1990 fair-housing grant draw (audit_grant) as the instrument for segregation (the multigroup entropy index), with direct general expenditure per resident as the outcome, deflated to real dollars. Because the grant was randomly assigned, paid a nonprofit rather than the city, and changed nothing else, the exclusion restriction is credible by design.
2. The estimation sample is the 40 large cities in the two participating states, using the 2000 and 2010 census years. I will control for 1980 and 1990 baseline values of log_pop, pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income and own_rate to improve precision, cluster standard errors by city, and also report the reduced-form effect of the draw on spending.
3. The main threat is a weak instrument: the first-stage F is about 2, so ordinary 2SLS estimates and t-tests would be biased toward OLS and badly mis-sized. I will therefore report Anderson-Rubin confidence sets as the primary inference, and I expect them to be wide.
4. I rejected waterways despite its strong first stage. Rivers and streams plausibly raise spending directly through bridges, flood control, stormwater systems and fragmented jurisdictions, so its exclusion restriction is doubtful.
5. Any estimate here is a local effect for large cities in two states whose segregation responded to the grant, and it may not generalize to all 2,600 cities.

CANDIDATES:
waterways | doubtful
audit_grant | plausible
INSTRUMENT: audit_grant

**Plan.** I will estimate the effect by instrumental variables, using `audit_grant` as the instrument for the segregation index and direct general expenditure per resident as the outcome. The sample is the 40 cities over 100,000 residents in the two participating states, observed in 2000 and 2010, after the 1990 draw. The grant was assigned by federal random draw and paid a nonprofit rather than the city government, which makes as-good-as-random assignment and exclusion plausible; I will control for `log_pop`, `pct_black`, `pct_hisp`, `med_income` and `own_rate`, include state-by-year effects, and cluster standard errors by city. I rejected `waterways`: although it strongly predicts segregation (1.5 points per stream), the program memo says every 1920 boundary stream became a jurisdiction line. That means more waterways produce more fragmented school districts and municipalities, which can change city spending directly and breaks exclusion. The main threat is weak identification: the first-stage F is about 2 and the sample is only 40 cities, so I will report the reduced form and Anderson-Rubin confidence intervals, which may be very wide. I will also state that the estimate is a local effect for large cities in two states, not for all 2,600 cities.

waterways | violated
audit_grant | plausible
INSTRUMENT: audit_grant

**Plan.** Neither candidate instrument supports a credible IV design, so I will not run IV as the headline estimate. `waterways` has a strong first stage (+1.5 index points per stream), but it fails exclusion. Streams drew the lines for school districts and municipalities, so waterways shift spending directly through jurisdictional fragmentation and Tiebout-style competition, not only through segregation. `audit_grant` was randomly assigned and plausibly excludable, since it funded a nonprofit and changed nothing else, but it covers only 40 cities and has a first-stage F of about 2. That would yield IV estimates biased toward OLS and Anderson–Rubin intervals too wide to be informative; I will report it only as a weak-IV-robust appendix check. The main design is therefore a city panel (1980–2010) regressing CPI-deflated direct general expenditure per resident on the entropy index, with city and state-by-year fixed effects. Controls are log_pop, pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income and own_rate, with errors clustered by city, plus an event-study check for pre-trends and Oster/sensitivity bounds. The main threat is time-varying confounding within cities, such as white flight or economic decline that both raises segregation and erodes the tax base, so I will present the result as a bounded association rather than a clean causal effect.

CANDIDATES:
waterways | violated
audit_grant | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: NONE

**Plan.** I cannot find a credible instrument here, so I would not anchor the study on IV. The main design is a city panel for 1980–2010 with city and state-by-year fixed effects. It regresses CPI-deflated direct general expenditure per resident on the entropy segregation index, controlling for log_pop, pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income and own_rate, with errors clustered by city, and reports a sensitivity analysis showing how strong unobserved confounding would have to be to overturn the result. Waterways predicts segregation strongly, but rivers raise spending directly through bridges, roads, flood control and drainage, and they shape a city's age, size and economic base, so the exclusion restriction fails. The 1990 audit_grant lottery is truly random, and the grant paid a nonprofit rather than the city, so it is plausibly excludable. However, it covers only 40 cities, moves segregation by 0.3 points and has a first-stage F of about 2, so I would report only its reduced form and an Anderson-Rubin confidence set as a side check, and I expect that set to be uninformative. The main threat to the panel design is time-varying confounding, such as white flight, suburbanization or a shifting tax base that changes both segregation and spending, along with reverse causality from spending to residential sorting; none of the many administrative item variables in the codebook resolves this.

waterways | violated
audit_grant | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: NONE

**Plan.** Neither candidate instrument supports a credible IV estimate, so I would not build the main estimate on IV. qob1 fails exclusion: Q1 births go disproportionately to teenage and unmarried mothers, so quarter of birth carries family background straight into 1979 wages, even with year- and state-of-birth fixed effects. building_draw is truly random and plausibly excludable, but its first stage is very weak (F ≈ 2, 0.03 years), and it covers only men born in 1939 in 20 rural counties, so 2SLS would be biased toward OLS and badly sized. I would report its reduced form and an Anderson–Rubin confidence set, which will likely be too wide to be informative, rather than a point estimate. The main analysis would regress log weekly wage on years of schooling with black, married, smsa, region, age_1980, and birth_state × birth-year fixed effects, with standard errors clustered by birth state. The main threat is unobserved ability and family background, so I would present the estimate as a bounded association, using Cinelli–Hazlett or Oster sensitivity analysis to show how strong omitted confounding must be to explain away the return.

CANDIDATES:
qob1 | violated
building_draw | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: NONE

**Plan.** I will estimate the return to schooling by 2SLS, using quarter of birth as the instrument. The first stage regresses years of schooling on `qob1`; the second stage regresses 1979 log weekly wage on fitted schooling. Both stages include year-of-birth and `birth_state` fixed effects, with `black`, `married`, `smsa` and `region` as optional controls, and I will cluster standard errors by state-of-birth × year-of-birth. The instrument works because school-entry rules and leave-at-16 compulsory schooling laws make first-quarter births complete about 0.13 fewer years, which across roughly 330,000 men should give a strong first stage; I will report it alongside a reduced form and an Anderson-Rubin interval. I set aside `building_draw` despite its genuine randomization: it covers only 1939 births in 20 counties of one state and has a first-stage F of about 2, so 2SLS with it would be biased toward OLS with unreliable inference. The main threat is the exclusion restriction: season of birth may correlate with family background, or relative-age effects may act on wages through channels other than completed schooling. I will probe this with covariate balance by quarter and by checking that later cohorts and degree holders, for whom compulsory schooling should not bind, show no reduced-form wage gap. The many administrative codebook items (`earnin_*`, `employ_*`, `milita_*` and others) have no as-good-as-random variation in schooling, so none is a candidate instrument.

CANDIDATES:
qob1 | plausible
building_draw | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: qob1

**Plan.** The standard quarter-of-birth instrument (qob1) fails exclusion here: the documentation says winter births go disproportionately to teenage and unmarried mothers, so family background can shift 1979 wages directly, not only through schooling. I would instead use building_draw, the county-level 1944 random draw of new consolidated high schools, among men born in 1939 in the 20 rural counties. I would estimate the effect of years of schooling on log weekly wage by IV, clustering standard errors at the county level (only 20 clusters, 10 treated, so I would use a wild-cluster bootstrap). The randomization and the "changed nothing else" note make exclusion and independence credible. The main threat is weakness: the first stage is about 0.03 years with F≈2, so 2SLS point estimates will be biased toward OLS and conventional t-tests are invalid. I would therefore report only weak-IV-robust Anderson–Rubin confidence sets, and say plainly that they may be very wide and that this subsample of rural 1939 births may not generalize to the full cohort.

CANDIDATES:
qob1 | violated
building_draw | plausible
INSTRUMENT: building_draw

**Plan**

1. I will estimate the return to schooling by two-stage least squares, instrumenting years of completed schooling with `qob1` (born January–March). Compulsory-schooling laws let those men leave school at 16 after fewer completed grades, about 0.13 fewer years on average.
2. Both stages will include year-of-birth fixed effects (built from `age_1980` and the census birth year) and `birth_state` fixed effects, with `black`, `married`, `smsa` and `region` as optional controls. I will report the first stage, its F-statistic and the reduced form, and use a single just-identified instrument rather than many quarter-by-year-by-state interactions. That avoids the many-weak-instrument bias toward OLS that Bound, Jaeger and Baker documented.
3. I considered `building_draw` because it is a true random assignment that changed nothing else in the drawn counties. However, it covers only men born in 1939 in 20 counties, and its first-stage F is about 2, so a 2SLS estimate from it would be badly biased and its confidence intervals unreliable.
4. The many administrative and survey items in the codebook (commute, housing, military, etc.) have no stated link to schooling. Several are post-treatment or measured long after 1980, so none is a credible instrument and none will be used as a control.
5. The main threat is the exclusion restriction for quarter of birth. Season of birth may affect wages through channels other than schooling, such as health at birth, mothers' socioeconomic background, or relative age in class. Small biases of this kind get magnified because the first stage is modest.
6. I will probe this in three ways: check that `qob1` is balanced on predetermined traits like `black` and `birth_state` composition; check that the reduced form is near zero among college-educated men, whom compulsory schooling should not bind; and report weak-instrument-robust (Anderson–Rubin) confidence intervals. The estimate should be read as a LATE for men whose schooling was constrained by compulsory-attendance laws.

CANDIDATES:
qob1 | plausible
building_draw | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: qob1

**Plan.** I will estimate the return to schooling by two-stage least squares, instrumenting years of completed schooling with `qob1` (born in January–March), in the spirit of Angrist and Krueger. The outcome is log weekly wage in 1979, and every stage includes year-of-birth and `birth_state` fixed effects; `black`, `married`, `smsa` and `region` serve only as robustness covariates, since marriage and residence may themselves respond to schooling. With about 330,000 men and a 0.13-year first-stage gap, I will use the single binary instrument rather than many quarter-by-year-by-state interactions, which avoids the many-weak-instrument bias Bound, Jaeger and Baker documented, and I will report the first-stage F alongside Anderson–Rubin intervals. I considered `building_draw` because its random assignment makes exclusion very plausible, but it covers only one small cohort-state cell and its first-stage F of about 2 makes it unusable; I will report it at most as a weak-IV-robust side check. The main threat is exclusion: season of birth may carry its own path to wages through family background (for example, the evidence of Buckles and Hungerman), health at birth, or relative age within the birth year. I will probe this with checks such as reduced-form "effects" in college graduates, who are unconstrained by leaving-age laws, and covariate balance by `qob1`. The administrative-style coded variables in the codebook are irrelevant to this design, and none qualifies as an instrument.

CANDIDATES:
qob1 | plausible
building_draw | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: qob1

1. I would not use quarter of birth (qob1) as an instrument, even with year-of-birth and state-of-birth fixed effects. The codebook notes that first-quarter births go disproportionately to teenage and unmarried mothers, so family background likely affects wages directly and the exclusion restriction fails.
2. Instead, I would use the 1944 random county draw (building_draw) as the instrument for years of schooling, with log weekly wage as the outcome. The sample would be the men born in 1939 in the 20 eligible rural counties.
3. Because counties were the unit drawn, I would cluster standard errors by birth county, which leaves only 20 clusters. That calls for wild-cluster bootstrap or randomization inference over the possible draws.
4. Random assignment makes independence credible, and the codebook says the draw changed nothing else, so exclusion is plausible. The estimate would be a LATE for men whose schooling responded to the new consolidated high school.
5. The main threat is weak relevance. The first stage is only about 0.03 years with an F-statistic near 2, so conventional 2SLS would be biased toward OLS and its confidence intervals would be wrong.
6. I would therefore report only Anderson–Rubin intervals that stay valid with a weak instrument, and I expect them to be very wide, possibly unbounded. I would tell the PI plainly that this design is credible but may be uninformative, and that full-sample OLS on schooling is descriptive only.

CANDIDATES:
qob1 | violated
building_draw | plausible
INSTRUMENT: building_draw

**Plan.** I would not claim a credible instrumental-variables estimate of the return to schooling from this dataset; I would report a clearly labeled descriptive OLS of log weekly wage on years of schooling instead. That regression would control for year-of-birth and state-of-birth fixed effects, black, smsa, region and age_1980, with married left out because it may itself be an outcome of schooling.

**Quarter of birth.** The natural instrument is qob1, the Angrist–Krueger quarter-of-birth design. The documentation, however, notes that winter births are disproportionately to teenage and unmarried mothers. That means quarter of birth carries family background that affects wages directly, so the exclusion restriction fails.

**The 1944 school draw.** building_draw is genuinely random and plausibly excludable. But it covers only men born in 1939 in 20 rural counties, and its first-stage F of about 2 makes 2SLS badly biased toward OLS. A weak-instrument-robust (Anderson–Rubin) confidence set from it would almost certainly be uninformative, so at most I would report it as an exploratory appendix.

**Main threat.** Ability and family-background bias in the OLS estimate remains unaddressed. The PI should therefore treat the result as an association, not a causal return. The administrative "items" variables are not candidate instruments: they are undefined, often post-treatment, and unrelated to how schooling was assigned.

CANDIDATES:
qob1 | violated
building_draw | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: NONE

**Plan.** I will estimate the return to schooling by instrumental variables, using `building_draw` as the instrument. The 1944 random draw assigned new consolidated high schools to 10 of 20 rural counties, so it is as-good-as-random and, per the documentation, changed nothing else in those counties. The estimation sample is men born in 1939 in those 20 counties: years of schooling is the endogenous treatment, log weekly wage in 1979 is the outcome, and the draw is the instrument, with standard errors clustered by birth county. I reject `qob1`, despite its stronger first stage. Q1 births are disproportionately to teenage and unmarried mothers, so quarter of birth is tied to family background that affects earnings directly, breaking the exclusion restriction. The main threat is weak identification: the first-stage F is about 2, the shift is only 0.03 years, and there are just 20 clusters. Conventional 2SLS would therefore be biased toward OLS with misleading standard errors, so I will report Anderson–Rubin confidence sets with wild-cluster bootstrap. I will present the result honestly as likely very imprecise, possibly an unbounded interval, rather than switch to the invalid but stronger instrument.

qob1 | violated
building_draw | plausible
INSTRUMENT: building_draw

**Plan**

1. I will not use `qob1`, the classic Angrist–Krueger instrument. The documentation says winter births go disproportionately to teenage and unmarried mothers, so quarter of birth likely affects 1979 wages through family background as well as through schooling, which breaks the exclusion restriction.
2. Instead, I will use `building_draw` as the instrument. It is the 1944 random draw that gave 10 of 20 rural counties a consolidated high school, and the documentation says it changed nothing else in those counties, so it is as good as randomly assigned and plausibly excludable.
3. The estimate is 2SLS on the men born in 1939 in those 20 counties. Years of schooling is the endogenous regressor, log weekly wage is the outcome, and `black`, `married`, and `smsa` are optional precision controls. Standard errors are clustered by birth county, because the draw was assigned at the county level.
4. The main threat is weak identification. The first-stage F is about 2, schooling rises by only 0.03 years, and there are only 20 clusters, so conventional 2SLS would be biased toward OLS and its confidence intervals would be unreliable.
5. I will therefore report Anderson–Rubin weak-IV-robust confidence sets, checked with wild-cluster or randomization inference over the possible county draws. I will state plainly if the resulting interval is too wide to say anything about the return to schooling.
6. OLS and the `qob1` IV estimate will be shown only as benchmarks, not as causal estimates. The ~290 administrative "items" variables have no plausible as-if-random variation in schooling, so I did not treat them as instruments.

qob1 | violated
building_draw | plausible
INSTRUMENT: building_draw

**Plan (six sentences)**

1. Neither available instrument supports credible IV identification of the effect of graduation on turnout.
   - `preschool_assign` is randomized and strong (19 points on graduation). But the program memo shows it also built externalizing-behavior and motivation skills, and similar skills raised adult turnout by 11–14 points in another experiment. That opens a direct path to voting, so exclusion fails.
   - `credit_waiver` is randomized and plausibly excludable. But it exists only for 1965-wave students who reached 12th grade, a small slice of the 123 children, and has a first-stage F of about 2. Two-stage least squares would be badly biased toward OLS, and any valid confidence interval would be uninformative.
2. I will therefore not report a point IV estimate. The headline causal result will be the randomized intent-to-treat effect of `preschool_assign` on voting in 1998–2008, interpreted as the effect of preschool, not of graduation.
3. For graduation itself, I will estimate a selection-on-observables model using only pre-treatment covariates: `female`, `iq_entry`, `parent_educ`, `father_home`, `ses_index`, `birth_year`, and `preschool_assign`.
4. That estimate will be paired with formal sensitivity analysis, such as Oster-style coefficient-stability bounds or Cinelli–Hazlett robustness values. These show how strong unobserved confounding would need to be to explain the association away.
5. As a supplementary check, I will report an Anderson–Rubin weak-IV-robust confidence set using `credit_waiver` within its eligible subsample. I expect it to be very wide and will present it as evidence of what the data cannot tell us, not as a finding.
6. The main threat is unobserved confounding, especially noncognitive skills that drive both graduation and voting, compounded by the tiny sample. Two secondary issues are error in name-and-date-of-birth voter-file matching and the fact that most codebook variables are post-treatment and must not be used as controls.

CANDIDATES:
preschool_assign | violated
credit_waiver | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: NONE

**Plan (no credible instrument is available)**

1. Neither candidate instrument supports a credible IV design, so I will not report an IV estimate. `preschool_assign` has a strong first stage (19 points), but it fails exclusion: the codebook says preschool built externalizing-behavior and motivation skills, which separately raise adult turnout by 11–14 points. `credit_waiver` plausibly satisfies exclusion ("changed nothing else"), but it exists only for 1965-wave students who reached 12th grade, a small subset of the 123. Its first stage is 4 points with F ≈ 2, so 2SLS would be badly biased toward OLS and its intervals would be meaningless.
2. I will instead estimate a selection-on-observables model of voted-1998–2008 on graduated-by-19. The model controls only for pre-treatment covariates: `female`, `iq_entry`, `parent_educ`, `father_home`, `ses_index`, `birth_year`/wave fixed effects, and `preschool_assign` (randomized, so a valid control), with robust standard errors.
3. I will exclude the many follow-up and administrative items (arrests, earnings, welfare, housing, and so on). Most are measured after graduation and would be bad controls, and many are missing before the 2013 migration or suppressed.
4. I will report Oster/Cinelli–Hazlett sensitivity bounds for how strong unobserved confounding would need to be to erase the effect. As a purely descriptive check, I will report an Anderson–Rubin test using `credit_waiver` in its subsample, not as an estimate.
5. The main threat is unobserved confounding, such as noncognitive skills or family engagement that drive both graduation and voting. With n = 123, imprecision and voter-file matching error on name and date of birth also matter, so the result should be framed as associational with explicit sensitivity analysis rather than causal.

credit_waiver | plausible
preschool_assign | violated
INSTRUMENT: NONE

**Plan (six sentences):**

1. The obvious instrument, `preschool_assign`, is randomized and strong (+19 pp graduation), but it fails the exclusion restriction. Perry-style preschool also shifted IQ, earnings, arrests, and social skills, and any of these could change voting directly, not only through graduation.
2. I will therefore use `credit_waiver` as the instrument. It was randomly drawn within the 1965-wave students who reached 12th grade, and it changed nothing except the diploma requirement, so exclusion is credible.
3. The estimate is 2SLS of the voted-1998–2008 indicator on graduation by 19, instrumented by `credit_waiver`. The sample is that 1965-wave senior subsample, and controls are pre-assignment covariates only (`female`, `iq_entry`, `parent_educ`, `father_home`, `ses_index`, `birth_year`, `preschool_assign`), added for precision. I will not use the many follow-up and administrative variables, which are post-treatment, imputed, or suppressed.
4. The estimand is a LATE: the effect for students in that one senior class who graduate only because the credit was waived.
5. The main threat is a weak instrument. The first stage is 4 pp with F ≈ 2 in what is probably a sample of a dozen or two students. Conventional 2SLS would be biased toward OLS with badly wrong standard errors, so I will report Anderson-Rubin confidence sets and the reduced form (waiver on voting) instead of t-tests.
6. I expect those intervals to be very wide and likely uninformative. If so, the honest conclusion is that this dataset cannot credibly identify the effect, and I would not fall back on the strong but excludability-violating preschool instrument or on OLS with controls.

CANDIDATES:
preschool_assign | violated
credit_waiver | plausible
INSTRUMENT: credit_waiver

**Plan.** Neither candidate instrument supports a credible IV design, so I will not report a 2SLS estimate. Assigning preschool (`preschool_assign`) was random and strongly shifts graduation (+19 pp), but it violates exclusion: the program also built psychosocial skills (fewer externalizing problems, higher academic motivation), and a separate experiment shows those skills alone raise adult turnout by 11–14 pp. `credit_waiver` plausibly satisfies exclusion, since it was a random draw that changed nothing else, but it exists only for 1965-wave seniors and has a first-stage F of about 2. With that F, 2SLS is badly biased toward OLS and any weak-IV-robust (Anderson-Rubin) interval will be uninformative, so it serves only as a descriptive reduced-form check. My primary estimate will therefore be a clearly labelled observational one: regress voting in 1998–2008 on graduation by 19, adjusting only for pre-treatment covariates (`female`, `iq_entry`, `parent_educ`, `father_home`, `ses_index`, `birth_year`, `preschool_assign`) via regression and propensity-score weighting. I will exclude all post-treatment adult outcomes (earnings, arrests, welfare, housing) and pair the estimate with formal sensitivity analysis (Oster bounds, E-values).
